newsitem.title: UK: Britain's N. Electric woos investors in bid fight.
newsitem.headline: Britain's N. Electric woos investors in bid fight.

text.p: British utility Northern Electric attempted to lure shareholders back to its side Tuesday to fight off CE Electric's takeover attempt after a British agency extended the deadline for the offer to Tuesday afternoon.

Northern's fate depended on winning back about 200,000 shares conditionally pledged to CE in the bitterly contested battle against the 782 million pound ($1.3 billion) bid from CE Electric, which is 70 percent owned by Omaha-based CalEnergy Co. Inc.
Northern urged shareholders to withdraw acceptances of the offer, which amounted to 650 pence a share.
Northern said that in the event of the CE bid lapsing, it was willing to talk with CE or another party "with a view to reaching agreement on an improved offer for Northern."

By agreeing effectively to "collapse" a rule that says a bidder cannot come back and bid for the same company within a 12-month period, Northern was opening the way for shareholders to withdraw their acceptances and reopen the debate about the value of the company, a Northern spokesman said.
Britain's Takeover Panel late Monday quashed an appeal by Northern against the extension of the deadline from last Friday.

CE said Monday it owned or had acceptances for 50.13 percent of Northern's shares -- enough to win control of the company -- compared with the only 49.77 percent it had at the end of the previous deadline on Friday.
"If 200,000 shares get withdrawn, it's possible for the bid to fail," a source close to the bid battle said.
In a further twist, the Financial Times reported that key institutional investor Prudential Corp. had attempted to persuade investors who already backed CE's offer to revoke their acceptances.
A Prudential spokesman was not immediately available for comment, and Northern said it did not know whether Prudential was trying to buy shares to defeat the takeover.
CE declined to give an update on the level of acceptances it had ahead of the deadline. "We are extremely optimistic," a spokesman said.

In rejecting Northern's appeal, the Takeover Panel referred to a discretionary payment of 250,000 pounds ($359,000) to one of the firm's advisers, Barclays Plc's BZW, that was not declared until Friday.
CE had raised concerns about the purchase of Northern shares last week by BZW and merchant bank Schroders.

"What is clear is that BZW had failed to inform the panel of the full facts and that during the last days of the offer it purchased shares in Northern whilst these facts remained undisclosed," the panel said in its statement.
"In all the circumstances, the panel therefore feels that justice requires it to allow CE a final opportunity to obtain sufficient acceptances to declare its offer unconditional," the watchdog added.
BZW, which as a result of not declaring the discretionary fee from Northern at the appropriate time will not now be paid that part, said it had done nothing wrong.

"BZW has at all times acted in good faith and has risked its own capital in support of Northern's defence. Our fee arrangement was in no way contingent upon the purchase of Northern shares and the panel has permitted this purchase to stand," a spokesman for the firm said.
It was not the first time such uncertainty has surrounded Northern's future since it was privatised along with its 11 regional electricity company peers in 1990.

In 1994 it was the first of the 11 companies to face a takeover and successfully fought off, partly with the help of an extraordinary 560 million pound ($800 million) defence package, a bid by conglomerate Trafalgar House, now owned by Norway's Kvaerner.
If CE's bid goes through, only two of the original regional electric companies Yorkshire Electricity and Southern Electric, will remain independent.
